meta.blurb: Elif lies awake at night with a head full of what-ifs. Over one growing season, her neighbour Mrs Hale teaches her, among the vegetable beds, how to ask better questions, take small steps and let go of what cannot be controlled. Calm, practical and kind.
meta.bible: Elif: a young woman in her late twenties who works in an office and worries a great deal; the book follows her from March to October. Mrs Hale: her older neighbour, a patient gardener with bad knees, who has worries of her own and still gets on with life. The allotment: Mrs Hale's plot of vegetables at Willow Lane Allotments, with a shed, a bench and a tap. Defne: Elif's sister. Mr Reeves: Elif's manager. The worry notebook: where Elif writes her worries down. Key ideas: worry is normal, calm breathing, sort worries into what can be done and what cannot, the next small step, possible is not probable, scheduled worry time, movement and sleep, talking to someone, thoughts are not facts, one row at a time, courage while still worried. When worry is heavy or constant, or affects sleep, health or daily life, talking to a doctor or counsellor is wise; this book is general information and is not a substitute for professional help. Voice and tone: gentle, practical, hopeful, with garden pictures; no studies or numbers are invented, and claims are hedged where evidence is mixed.

beats.scene: Elif lies awake in a dark bedroom, staring at the ceiling
beats.summary: Elif cannot sleep because her mind is full of what-ifs.

beats.scene: A woman walks hard on a gym treadmill and goes nowhere
beats.summary: Worry feels like work but often goes nowhere, like a treadmill.

beats.scene: Mrs Hale waves from over a fence beside a green vegetable plot
beats.summary: Her neighbour Mrs Hale notices Elif looks tired and invites her to the allotment.

beats.scene: Elif kneels in damp soil with a trowel beside Mrs Hale
beats.summary: Mrs Hale says worry is normal and has a job: it tries to protect us.

beats.scene: Elif places a hand on her chest and breathes beside the compost heap
beats.summary: Worry shows up in the body, and slow breathing can calm it.

beats.scene: Elif holds a seed packet and breathes slowly while Mrs Hale counts
beats.summary: Mrs Hale shows Elif to breathe out for longer than she breathes in.

beats.scene: Rows of tiny green weeds grow quickly around small vegetable seedlings
beats.summary: Worries grow like weeds, quickly and without being planted.

beats.scene: Elif writes in a small notebook on a wooden bench in the allotment
beats.summary: Writing worries down in a notebook makes them clearer and smaller.

beats.scene: A page with a line down the middle, labelled can do and cannot do
beats.summary: Elif sorts each worry into what she can act on and what she cannot.

beats.scene: Elif holds her phone and looks at a letter from the bank
beats.summary: Elif phones the bank about a bill, taking the smallest useful step.

beats.scene: Elif looks at dark clouds from a bench, then at a quiet sunlit path
beats.summary: Asking what is happening now brings her back from what-if thinking.

beats.scene: Elif reads old pages of her notebook beside a row of beans
beats.summary: Elif looks back at old worries in her notebook and finds that many never happened.

beats.scene: Elif writes on a page headed with the words the worst that could happen
beats.summary: Looking at a realistic worst case, and a plan for it, makes the fear less foggy.

beats.scene: Elif holds a weather map with a small cloud and a large sunny area
beats.summary: Something that is possible is not the same as something that is likely.

beats.scene: Mrs Hale waters one row of beans with a can while others wait
beats.summary: Mrs Hale waters one row at a time, and Elif learns to take a day at a time.

beats.scene: Elif sets a small kitchen timer on a table beside a mug of tea
beats.summary: Elif sets aside a fifteen-minute worry time each day and postpones her worries.

beats.scene: Elif digs a deep hole in dark soil with a spade
beats.summary: Absorbing physical work quiets the mind because it asks for her attention.

beats.scene: Elif and Mrs Hale walk briskly along a country lane in the morning
beats.summary: Regular walking and movement can improve mood and ease worry.

beats.scene: Elif places a notebook and a pen beside her bed under a small lamp
beats.summary: Elif keeps her notebook by her bed for midnight worries and stops looking at her phone.

beats.scene: A large cup of coffee beside a small cup of herbal tea
beats.summary: Too much coffee can make a person jittery and make worry feel worse.

beats.scene: Elif sits on a sofa and talks with her sister Defne over tea
beats.summary: Elif tells her sister Defne how she feels, and feels better for it.

beats.scene: Defne listens quietly with her hand on Elif's arm
beats.summary: Sometimes a person does not need advice, just someone who listens.

beats.scene: Elif frowns at a spreadsheet at her desk with a small mistake highlighted
beats.summary: Elif worries about mistakes at work, and Mrs Hale tells her that good enough is often enough.

beats.scene: Mrs Hale holds up a pile of dead tomato plants and laughs
beats.summary: Even Mrs Hale loses plants, and every gardener fails sometimes.

beats.scene: Elif looks at pictures of perfect gardens on a phone beside a messy plot
beats.summary: Comparing herself to other people's perfect-looking lives makes Elif feel worse.

beats.scene: Elif sits in a meeting while others do not look at her
beats.summary: Elif worries what people think of her, and learns that people notice us less than we imagine.

beats.scene: Elif lays out bills and coins neatly on a kitchen table
beats.summary: Facing money worries by listing the actual numbers and taking one step.

beats.scene: Elif holds a phone showing a long list of health symptoms
beats.summary: Searching worrying symptoms on the internet can make worry worse, and a doctor is the right person to ask.

beats.scene: Elif sits at the bedside of her father, holding a mug of tea
beats.summary: Elif cannot control her father's health, but she can visit him every week.

beats.scene: A grey sky with a sunny patch and a gardener who looks up
beats.summary: Uncertainty cannot be removed, but a person can learn to live with it.

beats.scene: Elif sits on a stone wall and watches storm clouds gather
beats.summary: Fighting a feeling often makes it stronger, so Elif practises accepting it.

beats.scene: Elif holds a thought bubble in her hand and looks at it carefully
beats.summary: A thought is not a fact, and she can say, I am having the thought that.

beats.scene: Elif gives a friend a warm hug and talks about her problem
beats.summary: Elif asks herself what she would say to a friend with the same worry.

beats.scene: Elif places a hand on her heart and smiles gently at the garden
beats.summary: Being kind to herself when things go wrong helps her recover more quickly.

beats.scene: Elif writes three lines in her notebook by lamplight at bedtime
beats.summary: At night she writes three good things from the day, which slowly shifts her attention.

beats.scene: Elif closes her eyes on the bench and touches the bark of a tree
beats.summary: Noticing the five senses brings her back into the present moment.

beats.scene: Elif stands at a screen in a meeting room with papers in her hand
beats.summary: The day of her big presentation arrives, and Elif's worries come back loudly.

beats.scene: Elif breathes slowly in the corridor before walking into the meeting room
beats.summary: She uses her tools and the talk goes well enough, though not perfectly.

beats.scene: Elif sits at her desk with her chin on her hand after the meeting
beats.summary: Elif does not replay the presentation again and again, but reviews it briefly and moves on.

beats.scene: Elif sits at a kitchen table with a cold cup of tea
beats.summary: A bad day returns and the worry comes back, but setbacks are a normal part of progress.

beats.scene: Elif paints a picture at a small table by a sunny window
beats.summary: Elif makes time for things she enjoys, because life is not only duty.

beats.scene: Elif and Mrs Hale share a simple meal on a bench
beats.summary: A regular routine and enough rest help keep her steady.

beats.scene: Mrs Hale hands a basket of vegetables to a neighbour at a front door
beats.summary: Helping others turns her attention outward and eases her own worry.

beats.scene: Mrs Hale rubs her sore knee while looking out over her rows
beats.summary: Mrs Hale has worries of her own, about her knees and about falling, but she keeps gardening.

beats.scene: Elif walks onto a stage in a small hall with a lit microphone
beats.summary: Elif accepts an invitation to speak at a small event, even though she still feels worried.

beats.scene: Elif sits with a kind doctor in a quiet room with a window
beats.summary: If worry is heavy or constant, or affects sleep and health, talking to a doctor or counsellor is wise.

beats.scene: Elif tastes a ripe red tomato in the sunshine, with a smile
beats.summary: Elif harvests her first ripe tomatoes and enjoys them without worry.

beats.scene: Elif turns the pages of her worry notebook in the golden light of autumn
beats.summary: Reading her whole notebook, Elif sees how much she has changed since March.

beats.scene: Elif and Mrs Hale clear the last plants from the garden beds
beats.summary: At the end of the season, Elif thanks Mrs Hale and she answers that Elif did the work.

beats.scene: Elif walks home from the allotment in warm evening light, calm and relaxed
beats.summary: Worry is normal; with small steps, kindness and acceptance, a person can worry less and live more.

B1B2: It is two in the morning and Elif is wide awake. Her mind is running through everything that could go wrong at work, with money and in her family.
Elif is exhausted, although she has done nothing but think. Worry, she realises, feels like work, but it is more like walking on a treadmill that never moves.
Mrs Hale, her older neighbour, sees the shadows under Elif's eyes over the garden fence. She invites her to spend Saturday helping at her allotment.
While they dig, Elif admits how much she worries. Mrs Hale says that worry is normal, because the mind is only trying to protect you from harm.
Elif notices that her shoulders are tight and her heart is racing whenever she worries. Mrs Hale tells her that slow breathing can help to calm the body.
Mrs Hale teaches Elif a simple exercise: breathe in for four counts and out for six. The longer breath out tells the body to slow down.
Mrs Hale points to the weeds that have appeared overnight between the seedlings. Worries, she says, are like weeds, because nobody plants them and they grow very fast.
Mrs Hale suggests that Elif write her worries in a notebook. Once they are on paper, they look clearer and smaller than they did in her head.
For every worry, Elif asks whether there is something she can do about it. If there is, she makes a plan, and if there is not, she practises letting it go.
One worry on her list is a bill that she does not understand. She takes a small step and phones the bank, and the problem turns out to be a simple mistake.
Elif learns to notice when her thoughts begin with what if. She stops and asks herself what is actually happening at this very moment.
After a month, Elif reads the first pages of her notebook again. To her surprise, many of the things she dreaded never happened, and others turned out to be much milder.
Mrs Hale suggests that Elif write down the worst realistic outcome, and then what she would do about it. Seeing a plan on the page makes the fear feel much less foggy and big.
Elif sees that she often treats possible things as if they were certain. Honestly guessing how likely a thing is turns out to be a very calming exercise.
The allotment looks enormous, but Mrs Hale only waters one row at a time. Elif decides to look at her days in the same way, instead of facing the whole year at once.
Mrs Hale says that some people set aside fifteen minutes a day to worry on purpose. When a worry arrives at another time, Elif writes it down and saves it for later.
When Elif digs, she has no space left in her head for worrying. Work with her hands gives her mind something simple and real to hold.
Mrs Hale walks to the allotment every morning, whatever the weather. Elif starts to take a short walk each day as well, and she feels calmer afterwards.
Night is the time when Elif's worries are always at their loudest. She keeps her notebook beside her bed, and she turns off her phone half an hour before she sleeps.
Mrs Hale points out that strong coffee can make a person feel shaky and nervous. Elif cuts down on it, and some of her anxious feelings fade.
Elif has hidden her worries from everyone, believing that they would think her weak. When she finally tells her sister Defne, she feels much lighter.
Defne does not try to fix anything or give long advice. She simply listens, and Elif realises that being heard is often enough.
Elif checks her work again and again, because she is afraid of a mistake. Mrs Hale tells her that perfect is not possible, and good enough is usually enough.
A cold night kills all of Mrs Hale's young tomato plants. She shrugs, laughs and says that every gardener loses plants, and she simply starts again.
Elif scrolls through pictures of other people's perfect lives and feels that she is falling behind. Mrs Hale reminds her that people only show their best photographs.
Elif worries all day about what her colleagues think of her. Psychologists have found that people tend to overestimate how much others notice them.
Money worries have kept Elif awake for longer than any other kind. She writes down every bill and every payment, and the page is less frightening than the fog in her head.
A small pain makes Elif search the internet, and soon she is sure that she is very ill. Mrs Hale says that a doctor is the right person to ask, not a search engine.
Elif is afraid for her father, who is old and has a cough. She cannot control his health, but she can visit him every week and make him laugh.
Elif wishes she could be certain about the future, but Mrs Hale says that is impossible. The weather is uncertain, too, and she plants her seeds anyway.
Elif has been fighting her anxious feelings and worrying about worrying. Mrs Hale tells her to let the feelings come and go like weather, without struggling.
When a frightening thought appears, Elif says to herself that she is having the thought that something will go wrong. This small distance shows her that a thought is not a fact.
Elif tries to imagine that her friend is having the same worry. She discovers that she would speak much more kindly to the friend than she does to herself.
Elif learns that being kind to herself does not mean she is lazy. When she makes a mistake, she says that she is learning, and she tries again the next day.
Before bed, Elif writes down three small things that went well that day. It is not magic, but it slowly teaches her mind to look for more than trouble.
When her thoughts spin, Elif names five things she can see, four she can touch and three she can hear. This simple game brings her attention back to the present moment.
The day of Elif's big presentation arrives, and all her old worries rush back. Her hands are shaking, and her mouth is dry.
In the corridor, Elif breathes in for four and out for six, and then she walks in. The presentation is not perfect, but it goes well enough.
After the meeting, Elif feels the urge to replay every word in her mind. Instead she writes down one thing to do better next time, and then she moves on.
A few weeks later Elif has a bad day, and all her old worries come back. She is afraid that she has lost everything she has learned.
Elif realises that she has stopped doing things just because she enjoys them. She starts painting again every Sunday, and her mind feels more open.
Elif sees that she feels steadier when she eats regular meals and goes to bed at the same time. A simple routine does not remove worry, but it gives her a firmer base.
Mrs Hale takes a basket of her vegetables to a neighbour each week. Elif joins her, and she finds that helping other people makes her own troubles seem smaller.
One day Mrs Hale admits that she worries about her sore knees and about falling. Elif sees that everyone worries, and that Mrs Hale has simply learned to keep going.
Elif is asked to speak at a small local event, and she feels the old fear. She says yes anyway, because courage does not mean the worry has disappeared.
Mrs Hale tells Elif that if worry is constant or stops you living, you should see a doctor or counsellor. This is common, there is no shame in it, and help is available.
The tomatoes that Mrs Hale planted again after the frost are finally ripe. Elif eats one in the sunshine, warm and sweet, and for a minute she thinks about nothing else.
In October, Elif reads her notebook from the first page to the last. She sees that her worries have not vanished, but they no longer rule her days.
On the last day of the season, Elif thanks Mrs Hale for everything. Mrs Hale only smiles and says that Elif did the digging, and that the soil is ready for next year.
Worry is part of being human, but it does not have to run your life. With small steps, honest questions, kindness and the courage to act, you can worry less and live more.
C1C2: At two in the morning, with the whole street asleep, Elif lay on her back and watched her mind run through every disaster it could invent. There was the meeting at work, the unpaid bills, her father's cough and the strange silence of a friend who had not replied to a message. None of it was happening at that moment, yet her heart was beating as though it were all arriving at once.

By morning she was exhausted, as though she had been labouring all night, and yet nothing had been solved or even begun. Worry, Elif reflected over her tea, resembles a treadmill in the way that it demands effort and delivers motion without any distance. It was a little comforting to put a picture to the feeling, because a feeling with a name is easier to look at.

Her neighbour, Mrs Hale, a small, brisk woman in a battered straw hat, leaned over the fence and observed that Elif looked as though she needed some fresh air. She had an allotment on the edge of town, she said, with far more weeds than one old woman could manage, and she would be glad of a pair of hands. Elif, too tired to invent an excuse and secretly curious about the garden, said yes at once.

As they dug side by side at the allotment, Elif confessed how much of her life she spent worrying, and she felt slightly foolish saying it. Mrs Hale replied that worry is not a defect but an old and ordinary instinct, a mind trying to protect its owner from danger, though it often becomes too enthusiastic for its own good. Knowing that she was not broken made the weight on her chest a little lighter.

Mrs Hale pointed out that worry is not only a thought but also a physical state, with tight shoulders, a clenched jaw and a heart that pounds as if it were being chased. The body and mind talk constantly to one another, she said, and if you slow down your breathing, the body will often tell the mind that the danger has passed. It is no cure for anything, but it is a good place to begin.

Mrs Hale taught her a plain exercise, in which she breathed in gently through her nose for a count of four and then out through her mouth for a count of six. The longer breath out seems to settle the body, Mrs Hale explained, although she made no claims for it except that it had helped her on many bad days. After five minutes, Elif found that the knot in her stomach had begun to loosen.

Between the delicate rows of seedlings, a green carpet of weeds had sprung up almost overnight, with no one having sown a single seed. Worries are just like that, said Mrs Hale, for nobody plants them on purpose and they spread effortlessly, whereas the plants we really want need patient care. Elif looked at her own thoughts in a new light, as a plot that needed regular weeding rather than a verdict on her character.

On the bench by the shed, Mrs Hale handed Elif a small notebook and suggested that she write down each worry as it arrived, in plain words. Elif was surprised to see that a worry that had seemed like a huge dark cloud at midnight looked, on paper, like three sentences about an ordinary problem. Putting a worry into words forces it to take a shape, and shapes are far easier to handle than fog.

Mrs Hale's next lesson was a single question to put to each entry in the notebook, namely whether there was anything that Elif could actually do about the matter. If there was, she should decide on a step and take it, and if there was not, her task was to practise setting it down, as one lowers a heavy bag at the end of a long walk. Elif found the first part easy enough, and the second one very difficult indeed, as most people do.

The bill that had been hanging over Elif for weeks seemed very large in her imagination, so she decided to take the smallest useful action available, which was to telephone the bank. The call lasted six minutes, and the problem turned out to be a clerical error that was corrected before she put down the phone. She sat staring at the receiver and wondering how many other worries were as flimsy as that one.

Almost every anxious thought, Elif discovered, began with the words what if, and each one dragged her into a future that did not yet exist. When she noticed one, she paused and asked herself what was actually happening at that moment, and the honest answer was usually that she was sitting safely in a chair with a cup of tea. The present moment, she thought, is surprisingly short of disasters, and it is the only place where she could ever act.

A month into the habit, Elif turned back to the first pages of her notebook and read her old fears with the curiosity of a stranger. Many of the disasters she had expected simply never took place, a few came in a milder form than she had imagined, and one or two had even turned out well. This proved nothing about the future, of course, but it cast serious doubt on the reliability of her inner prophet.

When a worry refused to shrink, Mrs Hale advised Elif to write down the worst realistic outcome, calmly and in detail, and then to note down what she would do if it came to pass. The exercise did not make the worst case pleasant, but it replaced a shapeless dread with a sequence of practical steps, and she saw that she could probably cope. Fear tends to feed on vagueness, and a plan is a very good way of starving it.

Her fears, Elif noticed, frequently dressed a mere possibility in the clothes of a certainty, so that a small chance of failure felt like a promised disaster. She began to ask herself how likely the event really was, in an honest and unromantic way, and she found that the answer was often rather low. Anything can happen, as Elif knew very well, but it does not follow that everything will.

The whole allotment looked daunting to Elif, but Mrs Hale never stared at all of it, and simply watered one row, then the next, until the work was done. Elif decided to treat her weeks in the same fashion, giving full attention to today's tasks and resisting the habit of carrying the whole of next month on her shoulders. It is hard to carry a year, but quite possible to carry an afternoon.

Mrs Hale described an odd-sounding trick that many people find useful, which is to set aside a short period each day, say fifteen minutes, in which to worry deliberately and thoroughly. When a worry crept into Elif's mind at any other hour, she wrote it in the notebook and told it firmly that it must wait for its appointment. To her astonishment, several of them never bothered to turn up at all, and the rest were over quickly.

Digging the potato bed was heavy work, and Elif noticed after a while that her mind had gone quiet without any effort at all. Absorbing activity, whether it is digging, cooking or building something, asks for just enough attention to crowd out the running commentary of anxiety, and it leaves one pleasantly tired. It is not the same as solving a worry, but it is an honest and healthy rest from one.

Mrs Hale walked to the allotment every morning, rain or shine, and she maintained that a brisk stroll was the cheapest medicine she knew. The evidence is generally encouraging that regular movement helps people feel calmer and sleep better, though it is not a substitute for proper help when worry becomes severe. Elif added a twenty-minute walk to her lunch break and soon noticed that her afternoons felt lighter.

At night, when the house was silent and there was nothing to distract her, Elif's worries were loudest and most convincing. She placed the notebook by her bed and wrote down whatever was troubling her, promising to look at it in daylight, and she stopped scrolling through her phone for half an hour before sleep. Her nights did not become perfect, but they became noticeably less crowded, and the mornings that followed were gentler.

Observing Elif's fourth cup of coffee before noon, Mrs Hale remarked mildly that caffeine can leave a person jittery, which is not helpful if the mind is already inclined to race. Elif cut down gradually, replacing some cups with herbal tea and water, and she was relieved to find that some of the shakiness that she had blamed on worry had come out of the pot. Not every symptom of worry, it seems, begins in the mind, and some of them begin in the cup.

For months Elif had hidden her worries from her family, assuming that they would think her weak or dramatic, and the secrecy had only made the burden heavier. When she finally told her sister Defne, over tea in a warm kitchen, she was astonished to hear that Defne had often felt the very same way. A worry shared is not necessarily solved, but it is almost always lighter to carry between two people.

Defne, to Elif's relief, did not interrupt with advice or hurry to fix anything, but simply listened with her whole attention and let the silence do its work. Elif realised that she had not needed solutions so much as company, and that being heard is itself a form of help. She decided to give the same gift to her sister whenever it was needed.

At the office, Elif checked her spreadsheets four and five times, terrified that a single wrong figure would expose her as a fraud. When she described this to Mrs Hale, the old woman snorted gently and said that nobody had ever grown a perfect vegetable, and that a good, honest crop was cause enough for celebration. Chasing perfection, Elif began to see, is a very effective way of becoming exhausted without becoming any better.

A late frost swept through the allotments one night and killed every one of Mrs Hale's young tomato plants, and Elif arrived expecting to find her in despair. Instead the old woman was cheerfully sowing new seeds, remarking that a gardener who has never lost a plant has never grown anything worth the trouble. Failure, in her view, was simply part of the information, and Elif wrote that down in her notebook.

Late one evening Elif scrolled through photographs of other people's immaculate gardens, holidays and careers, and she felt like the only person whose life was untidy. Mrs Hale reminded her that people post their best moments and hide the weeds, so that she was comparing the whole of her own life with a carefully chosen fraction of someone else's. Elif deleted the app from her phone for a month and was pleasantly surprised by the quiet.

In meetings, Elif was sure that every eye was on her and that her colleagues were privately judging each word she spoke. Psychologists have described a tendency known as the spotlight effect, in which people overestimate how much others notice about them, and the thought came to Elif as a great relief. Most of her colleagues, she realised, were far too busy worrying about themselves to be studying her.

Money was the worry that kept her awake most often, and it was also the one she had been avoiding the longest, afraid to look at the true figures. One evening she wrote out every bill, every payment and every pound of savings on a single page, and she saw that the situation was difficult but manageable. Looking directly at a problem is uncomfortable, but it is generally less alarming than the shape it takes in the dark.

A twinge in her side sent Elif hunting through websites in the middle of the night, and by dawn she had persuaded herself that she was seriously ill. Mrs Hale, who had once done the same, said gently that the internet lists every possibility but weighs none of them, and that a doctor is the proper person to consult about a real concern. This book offers only general information, and nothing here replaces a conversation with a professional.

Her father's cough was a worry that no list or breathing exercise could dissolve, for it concerned someone she loved and could not protect. After some thought she wrote it in the notebook under things she could not control, and beside it she listed what she could do, which was to visit him weekly and urge him to see a doctor. Love often asks us first to act as best we can, and then, which is harder, to accept the rest.

Elif longed for a guarantee that everything would turn out well, and she said so to Mrs Hale as the clouds gathered over the allotment. The old woman pointed out that no gardener has ever been promised good weather, and yet the seeds are sown every spring, because living means acting without certainty. Uncertainty cannot be cured, but tolerating it is a skill that can be learned.

Elif had become anxious about being anxious, and the more she fought her fear, the more fiercely it seemed to fight back. Mrs Hale suggested that she let the feeling arrive as one lets rain fall, without pushing it away or following it indoors, and wait for it to pass. It was a strange instruction at first, yet it was surprising how often the storm blew itself out.

Mrs Hale taught her to add a few extra words to a frightening thought, so that I will fail the exam became I am having the thought that I will fail. The change seems small, yet it creates a little space between Elif and the thought, and in that space she can notice that thoughts are only events in the mind and not forecasts of the future. She began to watch her worries drift past like clouds, without climbing aboard any of them, and she felt lighter.

When her thoughts turned harsh, Mrs Hale suggested that Elif imagine a close friend in her exact situation and consider what she would say to that friend. The answer was clear at once, for she would be warm, patient and reasonable, and she realised that she had been speaking to herself in a tone she would never use with anyone else. From then on she practised borrowing that kinder voice for herself, especially in the hours when she felt most alone.

Elif had always suspected that being gentle with herself would make her lazy, but she noticed that harsh self-criticism only made her frozen and afraid to try again. When she made a mistake, she began to acknowledge it, forgive it and take the lesson, and she recovered far more quickly than she used to. Kindness toward oneself, it seemed, is not an indulgence but a form of fuel.

Each night before sleep, Elif wrote down three things from her day that had gone well, no matter how modest, such as a warm cup of tea or a kind word from a stranger. The evidence for such exercises is modest and mixed, and Mrs Hale never pretended otherwise, but Elif found that her attention slowly began to notice good things as well as bad ones. It was a small change, and nobody else would ever have noticed it, but she was deeply glad of it.

In moments of panic, Mrs Hale told her, it can help to anchor the mind in the senses, by naming five things you can see, four you can touch, three you can hear and two you can smell. Elif tried it on a crowded train, quietly counting the red scarves, the cold rail, the hum of the engine and the smell of coffee, and her racing thoughts began to slow. The present moment, she discovered, was very much easier to bear than the imagined future.

On the morning of the presentation to the finance team, every worry she had ever had seemed to return at once, and her hands trembled as she collected her papers. She had practised alone and she had prepared well, yet knowledge of that did not prevent a flood of what-ifs from rising in her mind. It was exactly the moment for which she had been collecting tools all summer.

In the corridor outside the meeting room, Elif breathed in for four counts and out for six, named three things she could see, and reminded herself that she was having the thought that she would fail. She walked in with a pulse that was still fast, and she delivered a presentation that included one small stumble and was otherwise clear. Her manager, Mr Reeves, thanked her at the end, and the stumble, she saw, had been noticed by no one.

Afterwards, Elif felt the familiar pull to replay the whole presentation in her mind, hunting for every flaw and imagining what her colleagues must have thought. She gave herself five minutes, wrote down one thing that she would improve next time and one thing she was proud of, and closed the notebook. A calm review is useful and even wise, but an endless trial in the court of the mind is merely punishment.

A few weeks later, after a poor night and a sharp email, the old worries swept over Elif again with all their former force, and she sank into a gloomy conviction that she had made no progress at all. Mrs Hale only shrugged and said that weeds return every spring and that a good gardener is not the one with no weeds but the one who knows what to do about them. Setbacks, she added, are part of the road and not the end of it.

Looking back over her recent months, Elif saw that she had gradually abandoned everything that she did purely for pleasure, as though enjoyment had to be earned by first solving every problem. She took out her old paints and began to spend Sunday afternoons at the table by the window, with no purpose except to see what colours would appear. A life made only of duties leaves very little room in which to be calm.

With the help of a plain routine, Elif was eating proper meals, going to bed at roughly the same time each night and leaving her phone outside the bedroom. None of these habits was dramatic, and none of them removed her worries, but together they gave her a steadier footing from which to meet whatever came. Like a well-built fence, the routine was not interesting, but it kept things in place.

Every Thursday, Mrs Hale filled a basket with beans and lettuces and carried it round to neighbours who were lonely or unwell, and in the end Elif began to join her. Standing on doorsteps and receiving thanks, she noticed that her own thoughts turned outward for a while, and her troubles seemed more proportionate than they had in her bedroom. Kindness directed at others, it appears, has a way of returning to the giver.

One evening, rubbing her knee, Mrs Hale confessed that she lay awake sometimes, afraid of falling when she was alone at the allotment and unable to get up. Elif was surprised, for she had imagined that calm people did not worry, and she now understood that they simply live alongside their worries and carry on regardless. Mrs Hale had arranged a neighbour to check on her each week and then picked up her spade again.

When an invitation arrived asking Elif to give a short talk at a local community event, her stomach tightened and her first instinct was to refuse. She accepted instead, having learned that courage is not the absence of worry but the decision to act in its company, and that worry which is faced tends to shrink while worry which is avoided grows. The talk, when the evening came, was short, imperfect and, to her great surprise, entirely enjoyable for everyone.

Mrs Hale was careful to add that these habits are no substitute for professional care, and that worry which is constant, or which harms sleep, health or daily life, deserves a talk with a doctor or counsellor. There is no shame in that, she said, since anxiety is common and many people recover well with the right support. Elif noted down the name of her own doctor, in case she ever needed it.

By late summer, the tomatoes that had been sown again after the frost hung from the vines, heavy and glowing red, and Mrs Hale handed one to Elif without a word. It was warm from the sun and tasted of everything good in the season, and for a full minute she thought about nothing at all except its sweetness. It occurred to her that she was living, as opposed to merely preparing to live.

In October, as the leaves began to turn, Elif sat on the bench and read her notebook from the first page to the last, watching her handwriting grow calmer as the months passed. The worries had not vanished, for none of us can expect that, but she handled them differently, with a pause, a plan and a little kindness. She realised that she had been learning a skill, not waiting for a cure.

On the last Saturday of the season, as they cleared the beds and spread the compost for the winter, Elif tried clumsily to thank her old neighbour for all that she had taught her. Mrs Hale waved the words away and said that she had only handed over a spade, and that Elif herself had done the digging, every row of it. The soil, she added with a smile, would be waiting for both of them when the first warm days of spring returned.

Elif understood by then that nobody can expect to live without worry, and that the aim is not to destroy it but to give it its proper and limited place. Ask what you can do, take the next small step, let go of what you cannot control, speak to someone you trust, and remember to be kind to yourself along the way. The garden of a life is never finished, but it can be tended, and it can be enjoyed while it grows.
